Neonates of Ambystoma mexicanum emerge from their gelatinous egg capsules after an incubation period of approximately 12 days [ab = approximately 12 days] at a stable water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. Upon hatching, a process known as larval eclosion, the newly hatched larvae have a snout-vent length of 1.0 cm [Lb = 1.0 cm] and a wet weight of only 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], reflecting their lecithotrophic phase. These diminutive larvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days of life. The remarkably small size at hatching, with a body mass equivalent to just a few milligrams, contrasts sharply with the substantial adult dimensions this species can eventually attain. Under the same thermal conditions, at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the male axolotls reach sexual maturity, characterised by the onset of active gametogenesis and cloacal swelling, at approximately 548 days after hatching [tp = approximately 548 days after hatching]. This relatively protracted juvenile period, spanning nearly eighteen months, is a hallmark of the neotenic life history strategy that defines this iconic urodele. The long delay in reproductive activation is thought to reflect the extended period required for complete somatic growth under typical captive rearing regimes.

Laboratory colonies maintained at a constant temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C] demonstrate that female axolotls can attain an impressive maximum recorded lifespan of 17 years [am = 17 years], placing this species among the more long-lived salamanders. This extraordinary longevity is particularly notable given that the ultimate wet weight for mature females reaches 110 grams [Wwi = 110 grams], a relatively modest body mass for such an extended life span. Comparative data from other ambystomatid species suggest that this combination of moderate adult mass and extreme longevity is unusual, possibly linked to the paedomorphic retention of aquatic morphology and the associated reduction in terrestrial predation risk. The maximum total length, including the tail, recorded for large females in captivity can reach 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], although such large individuals are rare in laboratory settings and field-collected specimens typically remain smaller. These dimensions highlight the significant growth potential inherent in the species, which is constrained over a multi-decadal life history.

Reproductive effort in Ambystoma mexicanum is strongly influenced by the prevailing thermal regime, with most experimental data collected at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. Adult females, weighing approximately 25.3 grams, can produce a single clutch of approximately 1000 eggs [N_R_i = single clutch of approximately 1000 eggs] and typically spawn once per year [F_R_i = spawn once per year] at that specific temperature and body mass. The high fecundity, combined with the substantial maternal investment evident in the large, yolky eggs, underscores a reproductive strategy that prioritises high offspring number over per-offspring investment. At the same time, the consistent water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C] is critical for maintaining optimal metabolic performance and sustaining the high rates of gamete production observed in reproductively active adults.

Mature male axolotls exhibit a snout-vent length of 18 cm [Lp = 18 cm] at the onset of puberty, representing a significant size threshold that is attained after the prolonged juvenile growth phase. Achieving this body length is a reliable indicator of reproductive readiness, and males below this size rarely engage in amplexus or deposit spermatophores. The pubertal snout-vent length, when viewed in the context of the species' maximum total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], reveals that males must achieve approximately sixty percent of their potential ultimate body length before becoming reproductively viable. This substantial size at first reproduction is consistent with the pattern observed in many long-lived amphibians, where delayed maturity allows for the accumulation of sufficient somatic resources to support the energetic demands of courtship and mating. Field studies have noted that wild populations, although rare, show similar patterns of size at puberty, suggesting that the 18 cm [Lp = 18 cm] threshold is a robust life history trait rather than an artefact of captive conditions.

The neotenic life cycle of the axolotl, in which individuals remain permanently aquatic and retain larval features such as external gills, is intimately tied to its physiological tolerance for cool, stable water temperatures. At the standard laboratory temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the transition from freshly hatched larva to sexually mature adult follows a predictable developmental trajectory, with the acquisition of the 18 cm [Lp = 18 cm] snout-vent length at puberty constituting a critical milestone. The ultimate wet weight of 110 grams [Wwi = 110 grams] for females and the maximum total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm] represent the upper bounds of somatic growth, with most captive individuals asymptoting well below these maxima. The extended growth period, lasting years rather than months, is a direct consequence of the cool thermal regime that slows metabolic rates and extends developmental timelines. This slow pace of life, characterised by late maturity, low reproductive rate, and extraordinary longevity, aligns the axolotl with a classic slow life history strategy, making it an exceptional model for studies of ageing and developmental plasticity.
